name: Alfred Hitchcock
teaser: The Master of Suspense cameo'd in his own films because extras wouldn't show up for crowd scenes — he had to fill the frame himself.

exploreAction.targetName: Psycho (1960), the shower scene in isolation
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the shower scene and count the cuts. Hitchcock filmed 52 cuts in about 45 seconds — and never shows the knife touching skin. Notice how the stabbing is built entirely from suggestion and the score.

name: Akira Kurosawa
teaser: His 1950 Rashomon is why we call contradictory perspectives 'Rashomon-style' — the word entered everyday language because of one film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Kurosawa introduces the bandits with rain and horses before any dialogue. Then notice how each samurai gets a distinct entrance — he treated casting like composing a symphony.

name: Stanley Kubrick
teaser: Kubrick famously refused to fly and would not shoot in daylight unless the weather was perfect — which is why The Shining's exteriors took a year to film.

exploreAction.targetName: 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), the 'Dawn of Man' sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ape sequence with the sound off first. Kubrick cut the entire opening to 'The Blue Danube' — notice how the waltz turns evolution into choreography.

name: Martin Scorsese
teaser: Scorsese was a sickly asthmatic kid who couldn't play sports — so his father took him to the movies, and film became his playground.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous three-minute Steadicam shot where Henry walks his date through the back door of the Copacabana. Notice how the whole world bows to him — and how Scorsese later reuses the move as a fall.

name: Steven Spielberg
teaser: He once told a film student that the most important element in any shot is 'where to put the camera' — and then admitted he'd never found the rule for it.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first hour and note how often you SEE the shark versus how often you feel it. Spielberg hid the broken animatronic on purpose — necessity invented the horror of absence.

name: Federico Fellini
teaser: The word 'Felliniesque' exists because his films made dreamlike spectacle its own genre — surreal crowds, circus imagery, and faces no one else would cast.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening traffic-jam dream and count how many faces you recognize from later. Fellini cast his own crew and friends — the dream is a family reunion you don't know yet.

name: Ingmar Bergman
teaser: Bergman made Persona with a bare-bones crew of eight people on an island — and the film's famous split-screen moment came from an accident in the lab.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening montage — a nail hammered into a hand, a spider, a boy touching a blurred face. Bergman called Persona his 'one note' film: two women, one identity, zero escape.

name: Orson Welles
teaser: He directed Citizen Kane at 25 after convincing RKO he could do anything — then the studio buried it because its subject, William Randolph Hearst, threw his weight around.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the marriage montage — three years of a failing marriage in under a minute, told only through breakfast tables. Notice how each shot moves them further apart without a single line of dialogue explaining it.

name: François Truffaut
teaser: Truffaut was a juvenile delinquent who got out of reform school by promising to join the army — and instead became the loudest critic of French cinema, then its greatest young director.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final beach run and hold on the freeze-frame. Truffaut froze the film because he had no idea what happened to Antoine next — the image became the most famous ending in French cinema.

name: Jean-Luc Godard
teaser: Godard's Breathless used jump cuts because the film was too long — he simply chopped frames out of the middle of shots, accidentally inventing a new editing language.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the long bedroom scene and spot the jump cuts — moments where the image skips forward mid-motion. Godard cut to fix length; the roughness became the New Wave's signature.

name: Francis Ford Coppola
teaser: The studio tried to fire Coppola from The Godfather every week for the first month — then he filmed the opening wedding scene with hidden cameras and never looked back.

exploreAction.targetName: The Godfather (1972), the opening wedding scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wedding and notice how the FBI men frame the family through windows and doorways — surveillance baked into the very first scene, setting up the whole saga.

name: David Lynch
teaser: Lynch studied painting before film and calls his movies 'moving paintings' — he wrote the script for Eraserhead in a basement while his wife was pregnant.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening without trying to solve it. Lynch wants the feeling first: the pink light, the jitterbug, the crash. Notice how the camera keeps drifting toward things nobody explains.

name: Christopher Nolan
teaser: Nolan wrote Memento backwards — literally started from the last scene — because he wanted the audience to feel his protagonist's memory loss.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening backwards sequence and track the Polaroid rewinding. Nolan shot the color scenes in reverse and the black-and-white scenes forward, so the endings of both strands meet in the middle.

name: Quentin Tarantino
teaser: Tarantino learned film by working in a video store — he has admitted that the store's library was his film school.

exploreAction.targetName: Pulp Fiction (1994), the opening diner scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the diner conversation and notice how the 'Royale with Cheese' dialogue tells you everything about character without plot. Tarantino's rule: small talk is never small.

name: Paul Thomas Anderson
teaser: Anderson wrote Magnolia's famous 'rain of frogs' ending first, then built an entire film around the right to use it — he's said he just needed a movie worthy of the scene.

exploreAction.targetName: There Will Be Blood (2007), the opening 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wordless opening — Daniel Plainview digging alone in a hole. Anderson holds the shot for minutes with no dialogue. Notice how the film trusts silence the way most movies trust speech.

name: Wes Anderson
teaser: Anderson's symmetrical style started as a happy accident — he kept centering shots because he didn't know how else to frame a scene, and it became his signature.

exploreAction.targetName: The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014), the opening 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening and count the aspect ratios — Anderson changes the frame shape for each time period. The pink hotel, the model trains, the symmetry: notice how style IS the story here.

name: David Fincher
teaser: Fincher is famous for 60-plus takes per scene — he once shot a single Michael Douglas moment in The Game 57 times because the blink wasn't right.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening credits — scribbled notebooks, cut fingers, a man crossing out words. Fincher built the killer's mind in two minutes of pure montage before a single line of plot.

name: Ridley Scott
teaser: Scott studied at the Royal College of Art and worked in advertising before film — which is why his movies look like the most expensive commercials ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: Blade Runner (1982), the opening flyover of Los Angeles
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening cityscape and notice the mix of 1940s art deco with 2019 sprawl. Scott built the future from the past — flames, neon, and rain everywhere, a Los Angeles that never saw daylight.

name: James Cameron
teaser: Cameron wrote the treatment for the first Terminator while sick with a fever dream in Rome — he literally dreamed the endoskeleton rising from fire.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Ripley is basically fired for telling the truth, then the marines' drop. Cameron turns the horror of the first film into a war movie: notice how much time he spends on the grunts before the action.

name: George Lucas
teaser: Lucas wrote Star Wars as a 1970s homage to Flash Gordon serials, and every studio rejected it until Fox took the risk — the film's merchandising alone rewrote Hollywood's business model.

exploreAction.targetName: Star Wars (1977), the opening crawl and first scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening scroll and then the chase — Lucas opens mid-story, in media res, like a serial from 1938. Notice how the very first shot is a spaceship flying UP, something audiences had never seen.

name: Sergio Leone
teaser: Leone's 'spaghetti westerns' were filmed in Spain with mostly European crews — and Ennio Morricone wrote the scores before filming, so Leone cut the movies to the music.

exploreAction.targetName: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966), the final duel
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the three-way standoff — fifteen minutes of close-ups, no dialogue, just breathing and Morricone's score. Leone built the entire film toward this circle of faces.

name: Terrence Malick
teaser: Malick vanished from filmmaking for 20 years after Days of Heaven — he was a Rhodes scholar and philosophy teacher who simply stopped making movies, then returned as mysteriously as he left.

exploreAction.targetName: Days of Heaven (1978), the opening train sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — golden wheat, a fire, a train, almost no dialogue. Malick shot mostly at 'magic hour' and the crew had maybe 20 minutes of usable light a day. The film is made of sunsets.

name: Andrei Tarkovsky
teaser: Tarkovsky burned a real forest for the ending of Andrei Rublev — the Soviet state gave him 10,000 liters of fuel to do it, and he used every drop.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — long shots of a damp, ruined industrial town. Tarkovsky made the Zone with almost no special effects: the 'impossible' scenes are done with camera placement and patience. Notice how time slows down.

name: Wong Kar-wai
teaser: Wong shot In the Mood for Love over 15 months, often without a script — the actors learned their lines on the day, and the film's rhythm came from that improvisation.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Mood for Love (2000), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Wong frames the two neighbors through doorways and hallways — always at a distance, always in motion. The film's longing lives in the space BETWEEN the actors.

name: Hayao Miyazaki
teaser: Miyazaki draws most key animation himself and refuses to use CGI for characters — he retired and un-retired so many times the Japanese press stopped counting.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the parents turning into pigs happens almost casually. Miyazaki said he made this film for the daughters of his friends: notice how Chihiro's fear is drawn with real, patient detail.

name: Satyajit Ray
teaser: Ray made his first film on money borrowed from his mother, with a crew of amateurs — Pather Panchali became the film that put Indian cinema on the world map.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the train that Apu chases becomes the film's central metaphor. Ray shot in a real village with non-actors and a borrowed camera; the naturalism changed how the world saw Indian film.

name: Bong Joon-ho
teaser: Bong keeps a strict rule that his films must work on two levels at once — 'Once you overcome the one-inch tall barrier of subtitles, you will be introduced to so many more amazing films.'

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening half hour — the Kim family folding pizza boxes in their semi-basement. Notice how every shot is built on vertical movement: the family climbs into the rich house, and the movie climbs with them.

name: Denis Villeneuve
teaser: Villeneuve made Arrival after years of refusing big studio offers — he only accepted when the script's heart, grief, couldn't be removed from the sci-fi package.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the montage of Louise's life with her daughter plays before you know what it is. Villeneuve plants the film's twist in the first five minutes and counts on you not seeing it.

name: Kathryn Bigelow
teaser: Bigelow was a painter at the San Francisco Art Institute before film — and the first woman to win the Best Director Oscar, for a film about bomb disposal.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hurt Locker (2008), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening disarming scene — Bigelow shoots it with documentary urgency and almost no score. Notice how the silence does the suspense work the music usually does.

name: Greta Gerwig
teaser: Gerwig wrote Lady Bird from her own Sacramento adolescence and cast her own mother's house as the set — the family home in the film is literally her childhood house.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening car ride — mother and daughter argue about music and everything else. Gerwig's dialogue overlaps like real families: notice how people talk OVER each other, not at each other.

name: Sofia Coppola
teaser: Coppola wrote Lost in Translation in a Tokyo hotel room while jet-lagged — the entire film is essentially the feeling of being awake at 3 a.m. in a foreign city.

exploreAction.targetName: Lost in Translation (2003), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Scarlett Johansson looking out a hotel window, Bill Murray in the back of a cab. Coppola barely explains anything; the film IS the feeling of not belonging. Notice the neon.

name: Spike Lee
teaser: Lee directed Do the Right Thing on a $6.5 million budget and shot the hottest day in Brooklyn history — the heat in the film is real, 100-degree street temperature.

exploreAction.targetName: Do the Right Thing (1989), the opening credits
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening credits — Rosie Perez dancing to 'Fight the Power' in a series of hard cuts. Lee introduces his whole world, heat and anger, before a word of plot. Notice how the music IS the thesis.

name: Joel Coen
teaser: The Coen brothers alternate who takes director credit per film — 'Joel and Ethan' share everything, and neither will say who did what.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Jerry's desperate phone call, then the snow. The Coens frame Minnesota politeness as a crime scene waiting to happen. Notice the 'true story' claim they later admitted was a lie.

name: John Ford
teaser: Ford shot The Searchers almost entirely in Monument Valley, a place he treated as his personal studio — he framed its buttes so often they became the visual shorthand for the American West.

exploreAction.targetName: The Searchers (1956), the final doorway shot
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous final shot — Ethan framed in a doorway, turning away from the family he saved. Ford's doorways are cages: the last image is the loneliest in cinema.

name: Billy Wilder
teaser: Wilder fled Nazi Germany with almost nothing, learned English by listening to radio, and became the greatest writer-director of Hollywood's golden age — his dialogue is still quoted as the gold standard.

exploreAction.targetName: Some Like It Hot (1959), the last line
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending — 'Nobody's perfect' is one of the most quoted lines in cinema, but the buildup to it is the joke. Notice how Wilder plants a dozen gags in the final chase scene.
